analysis.one_liner: Requires large social media and gaming platforms to shield minors from addictive designs, harmful content, and targeted ads.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee and full committee by voice vote in 2024 with 64 bipartisan cosponsors, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a legal 'duty of care' on the biggest social media and gaming companies to prevent and mitigate harms to minors — anxiety, depression, eating disorders, substance use, bullying, sexual exploitation, and exposure to ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol. It would require platforms to offer minors tools to turn off addictive features like infinite scrolling and autoplay, opt out of algorithmic recommendations, and limit time on the app, with the most protective settings on by default and parental controls for accounts known to belong to young children. It would also require annual independent audits of how platforms affect minors, fund National Academy of Sciences research on social media harms, and let users of any age switch to a feed that is not ranked using their personal data. Enforcement would sit with the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and children under 17. The bill would require platforms to default minors into the most protective settings, give families controls over purchases, contacts, screen time, and algorithmic feeds, and force large platforms to disclose how much time minors spend on them and what risks their design features pose.

how_it_helps.text: The largest platforms would face a legal duty to exercise reasonable care to prevent harm to minors from anxiety, depression, eating disorders, compulsive use, bullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol.

Platforms would have to give known minors one-click safeguards to limit who can contact them, turn off addictive design features like infinite scrolling and autoplay, and opt out of personalized recommendation algorithms — with the most protective settings on by default unless a parent changes them.

Parents would get tools to manage a child's account, restrict in-game purchases and financial transactions, and view or cap total time spent on the platform, and must give verifiable parental consent before a child under 13 starts using a platform.
Platforms with more than 10 million U.S. users would have to publish annual public reports on risks to minors, based on independent third-party audits with full access to internal data.
The FTC would commission at least five comprehensive National Academy of Sciences studies on social media's effects on minors, and platforms could be ordered to supply data for the research.
Users of any age could switch from an 'opaque' algorithm that ranks content using their personal data to an 'input-transparent' feed, and could not be charged differently for making that choice.

analysis.who_pays: Large social media, gaming, and video-streaming companies. They would bear the cost of redesigning features, running audits, building parental tools and reporting systems, and defending against FTC and state enforcement — costs that fall hardest on platforms whose business models depend on maximizing engagement and ad targeting of young users.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and gaming platforms

drawbacks.text: A broad legal 'duty of care' covering vaguely defined harms like depression and anxiety could push platforms to over-restrict what minors can see and say — shutting down entire categories of content, including content helpful to vulnerable teens — rather than risk legal liability. Civil liberties groups raised this objection to companion versions of the bill.

To comply, platforms would likely need to know which users are minors, which can mean collecting or inferring more age data about everyone — the bill only forbids requiring new age collection (Section 113(b)) and instead orders a study of device-level age verification, leaving that question open.

State attorneys general could sue platforms over the safeguards and disclosure provisions, creating a patchwork of lawsuits that could be used for political ends and that could pressure platforms into removing lawful content.

The parental tools required for children under 13 — enabled by default — include viewing account settings and time metrics, which some child-privacy advocates warn can expose kids who depend on platform privacy, such as young people in unsupportive homes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and popular: limiting addictive design defaults, blocking ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, and alcohol to minors, and forcing the biggest platforms to disclose their effects on children. The design is narrower than the Senate-passed version of KOSA — the duty of care applies only to companies with $2.5 billion in revenue or 150 million users, states cannot sue under state law on the duty-of-care section, and no age-verification mandate is imposed. The main honest concern is the first one: a duty of care written around mental-health harms gives platforms a strong incentive to keep minors away from any content a court might later call harmful, which can shade into censorship of legitimate speech. On balance the bill trades a genuine over-censorship risk for enforceable limits on engagement-driven design aimed at kids.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2024, cleared a House subcommittee in May, and was approved as amended by the full Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2024 — but House leadership never brought it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Gus Bilirakis introduced the bill on April 9, 2024, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee.
It gathered 64 cosponsors split evenly between 32 Democrats and 32 Republicans.
On May 23, 2024, the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce considered and amended the bill and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.
On September 18, 2024, the full Energy and Commerce Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported, as amended, by voice vote — meaning no member forced a recorded vote against it.
After that, the record shows no further action: the bill was never debated on the House floor and never received an up-or-down vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

A Senate version of the Kids Online Safety Act had passed the Senate 91-3 in July 2024, meaning the House bill's fate rested entirely on whether House leadership would schedule it — which never happened.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large social media and gaming platforms are better off: they avoid for now the duty of care, mandatory protective defaults, third-party audits, and algorithmic opt-outs the bill would have imposed, while the families the bill was written for get nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and gaming platforms

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan — 32 Democratic and 32 Republican cosponsors, and the bill cleared subcommittee and full committee by voice vote — but opposition from parts of the tech industry and civil liberties groups coincided with House leadership's decision never to schedule a floor vote.

industries.note: Companies earning $2.5 billion or more or reaching 150 million users would face a duty of care, mandatory protective defaults for minors, annual third-party audits, and FTC and state AG enforcement. Their revenue depends on engagement and ad targeting of young users, which the bill directly constrains — and their interest in avoiding those constraints ran against parents' interest in protections. Stalling the bill preserved that revenue model.

Games with user communication or in-game purchases are covered: minors would get usage safeguards, parents could restrict microtransactions (including loot-box-style 'surprise mechanics'), and the bill explicitly excludes purchases made with currency earned through gameplay. Game makers gain a carve-out from gameplay interruptions but face new purchase controls and reporting duties.

Platforms would be barred from advertising narcotic drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to known minors, and minors could opt out of personalized recommendation systems — shrinking the audience data available to ad targeting aimed at young users.

Streaming services whose content is preselected rather than user-generated are deemed compliant with relatively light requirements (profile controls, autoplay limits, no harmful ads to minor profiles), locking in a lighter-touch regime for them relative to social media.
